analysis.one_liner: Strips federal courts of power over religion, privacy, reproduction, and marriage cases, leaving those to state courts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2006 by Rep. Ron Paul with six Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the Supreme Court and all other federal courts from deciding any case about state or local laws on religion — such as school prayer or religious displays — and from deciding any privacy claim involving sexual practices, sexual orientation, or reproduction, including abortion, or any equal-protection claim to marry regardless of sex. It would also make federal decisions on those topics no longer binding on state courts, so each state's courts and legislature would have the final word. Finally, it says any judge who defies these limits could be removed, and it forbids federal courts from ordering states to spend money or interfering with state lawmaking.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, and people who want decisions about school prayer, religious displays, abortion, and marriage made by their state legislatures and courts rather than by federal judges. Backers argue the Constitution gives Congress power to set the limits of federal court jurisdiction and that these matters belong to the states under the Tenth Amendment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State governments deciding religion, abortion, marriage

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Supreme Court and every federal court from hearing any claim involving state or local laws on the free exercise or establishment of religion, and from hearing any privacy claim related to sexual practices, orientation, or reproduction, or any equal-protection claim to marry without regard to sex or sexual orientation.

Declares that any federal court decision on an issue removed from federal jurisdiction is no longer binding precedent on state courts, so earlier federal rulings on those topics could not be enforced through state courts.
Prohibits federal courts from issuing any ruling that appropriates money, imposes taxes, or interferes with the legislative functions or administrative discretion of the states.

States in its findings that Congress has authority under Article III to make exceptions to federal court jurisdiction and that decisions on religion, family relations, education, and abortion have wrested issues from state and local governments.

analysis.who_pays: People whose rights claims would no longer be heard by any federal court: a religious minority challenging a school prayer or religious-display law, a woman seeking an abortion in a state that bans it, or a same-sex couple challenging a marriage ban would have to rely entirely on state courts, and federal precedents on those topics would no longer bind those courts.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal rights protections

drawbacks.text: It removes federal constitutional review entirely for church-state disputes and privacy claims: state and local governments could promote religion, restrict abortion, or ban same-sex marriage without any federal court recourse, and existing federal rulings on those topics would stop binding state courts.

It provides that a judge who violates the limits is subject to removal by the President under rules Congress establishes, alongside impeachment — a removal path outside the Constitution's impeachment process, which critics of jurisdiction-stripping measures have pointed to as conflicting with federal judges' life tenure.

The bill's stated goal is returning these questions to elected state governments, but that same mechanism means an individual's right to challenge a state law would depend on which state they live in, replacing one nationwide standard with fifty different ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's appeal is real for people who believe unelected federal judges have taken too many decisions away from state voters, and Congress does have textual authority under Article III to set the jurisdiction of lower federal courts. But the cost falls on individuals whose constitutional claims — church-state separation, reproductive privacy, marriage equality — would no longer be heard anywhere in the federal system, and the state-level outcome would vary by geography. The President-removal provision also raises separation-of-powers problems. On balance the bill trades federal rights protection for state control, and the people most affected would be those in states whose governments restrict these rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Paul introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Six Republican House members cosponsored the bill; no action beyond the referral was ever taken, and no vote occurred before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on federal courts to protect church-state separation, reproductive privacy, and marriage rights are better off, since the bill would have removed that recourse had it passed. Nothing else changed: the bill was too narrow in support to move, so no group gained anything concrete from its death.

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 29, 2006 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 6 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the members named at introduction: Reps. Tancredo, Sam Johnson of Texas, Jones of North Carolina, Sullivan, and Duncan.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no markup, hearing, or vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven House members behind the bill were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored it; no Democrats are recorded opposing it either, since the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: State and local governments seeking to regulate religion, reproduction, and marriage
industries.note: The bill hands these governments final authority over school prayer, religious displays, abortion, and marriage rules, freed from federal court review. Their gain comes directly at the expense of individuals in those states who could no longer bring those claims to a federal court.

Groups seeking to advance religion in public institutions and restrict abortion and same-sex marriage would gain a legal environment where federal precedents on those topics no longer bind state courts.

The bill strips the federal courts of jurisdiction over a broad set of civil-rights claims and threatens removal for judges who rule anyway. Preserving an independent federal forum for individual claims also serves the public that uses it.
